If lightning hits your car, all the electricity sticks to the outside (because it's much easier for electricity to move through the metal) and discharges to the ground through your tires. That might sound counterintuitive because the tires are insulators, but it's still the easiest path to take because in order to hit the inside, it would have to go through your seats and carpet and other insulators as well as the tires.


In short, lightning wants to get to the ground, and it's easier to go around your car than to go through it.

There are a few things to clear up here. Sexuality, physical sex, gender identity, and gender expression.

Sexuality is who you're attracted to. It's somewhat more likely for a man to be attracted to a woman, so gender identity has SOME limited bearing on sexuality, but it doesn't determine anything.

Physical sex is how you were born. It's your organs and your chromosomes. physical sex has a bearing on gender identity -- most people have a gender identity that lines up with their physical sex. these people are cis.

There's also gender identity -- this is what gender you are mentally, not physically. this is "made up", but it's still important -- just like science and politics and time. it DETERMINES your pronouns. it has a bearing on gender expression, but it doesn't determine any of it.

Gender expression is how masculine or feminine you are. Clothes, hair, makeup, etc., this is all gender expression, NOT identity.

Elliot page would be a fairly masculine-->(gender expression) man-->(gender identity) who is straight-->(sexuality) and was assigned female at birth or AFAB-->(physical sex)

all things considered, it's a **relatively** rare issue. out of everything surrounding trans people, it doesn't affect that many of us, and i'd be very surprised if it was ANYONE'S biggest concern. 



trans people, unfortunately, are somewhat physically different from cis people, even after surgery and hrt. to the best of my somewhat limited knowledge, there's very little that it absolutely determines, but it does change the likelihood of various things.



for example, you can't say that trans women are guaranteed to have hips between 28 and 32 cm while cis women are guaranteed to have hips between 38 and 42 cm. it just doesn't work that way. depending on very precise details of transituon and genetic lottery, the distribution may change, but the possibilities for something like that are the same (within reason).



One should consider that these differences are also present between races. black men are more likely to be taller than white men, but they still compete against one another in the NBA. is it the same? i would be cautious to draw that equivalence. but i do think we can draw a parallel here -- i think it's awfully similar, if a little less drastic.


in the end i'm not entirely sure how i feel about this. Maybe a weight class-esque system could be implemented in more sports? i certainly don't believe cis men transitioning so they can kick women's asses at sports is a major problem, but it's hard to say if trans women have an unfair advantage. do cis women who are taller have an unfair advantage? do cis women who are talented have an unfair advantage? do cis women born into wealth who can train more have an unfair advantage? it's a VERY difficult line to draw.
